notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Isaiah 50, drawn from the sources I was able to reach. I note at the end which traditions and perspectives I could not reach due to search/fetch limits.

---

## ISAIAH 50 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### Overview of the Chapter

**v. 1–3** — The LORD (Yahweh) addresses doubting Zion, rebutting the claim that He has permanently cast off His people. **v. 4–9** — The third "Servant Song": the obedient Servant (understood by Christian interpreters as the Messiah, Jesus) speaks of His submission, suffering, and vindication. **v. 10–11** — A closing exhortation contrasting trust in the LORD with reliance on self-made "fire."

- Precept Austin notes the chapter's threefold structure: "The perverse servant (Isa 50:1-3); The perfect Servant (Isa 50:4-9); The pattern Servant (Isa 50:10-11)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-50-commentary)
- Gill summarizes: "This chapter is a prophecy of the rejection of the Jews, for their neglect and contempt of the Messiah; and of his discharge of his office as Mediator." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)

---

### v. 1 — "Where is your mother's certificate of divorce…?"

**Traditional reading:** God challenges Israel's/Zion's claim to have been abandoned. He asks them to produce a bill of divorce or prove He sold them to creditors. Neither document exists — their separation was caused by their *own* sins, not God's unfaithfulness.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Judah's children wrongly supposed themselves altogether cast off. "They had, in fact, by their transgressions… wilfully divorced themselves… but no sentence had gone forth from him to bar reconciliation and return." God has not exercised a parent's right to sell children to creditors; the Babylonians are not their rightful owners. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Gill (Baptist):** The "mother" is the Jewish church or synagogue. The Lord challenges them to produce a bill of divorce — if one exists, it would show the fault was theirs, not His. "Behold, for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves… they had sold themselves to work wickedness, and therefore it was but just that they should be sold." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Both questions imply a negative answer. "Jehovah had not formally repudiated the wife (Judah) whom he had chosen… as he had done her sister Israel (Jeremiah 3:8). He had no creditors among the nations who could claim her children. The divorce, the sale, were her acts and not His." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "There were some who said God had put away, like a divorced woman, His ancient people… But He says, 'It is not so. Where is the bill of divorcement? To whom have I sold you?'… the nation… had lost the favor of God — not because of His fickleness, but because their sins had cried aloud for justice." (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons47/sermons47.xxxi.html)
- **Guzik (Enduring Word, charismatic/evangelical):** "God speaks to a doubting Zion, 'You say I don't care about you anymore. You say I have divorced you. Very well then, produce the document. But there is none because I have not divorced you.'" Quotes Redpath: "God cannot divorce those whom He has taken into covenant relationship with Himself." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)
- **Wiersbe (via Precept Austin, evangelical):** God is "a constant lover." The Mosaic permission for divorce (Deut 24:1-4) prevented a divorced woman from returning to her former husband. God had divorced the Northern Kingdom (Jer 3:8) but had not divorced Judah — He had only permitted chastening. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-50-commentary)
- **MacArthur (via Precept Austin):** "The unconditional promises of the Davidic Covenant (2 Sam 7:12-16) precluded such a divorce for Judah, although there would be a time of separation (cf. Isa 54:6-7)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-50-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — "Why was no one there when I arrived? … Is My hand too short to redeem you?"

**Traditional reading:** God came to His people (through prophets, deliverance, and ultimately through Christ) but found no welcome — no man to answer His call. This is not due to any lack of divine power; He who dried up the Red Sea and turned rivers to wilderness can surely redeem.

- **Gill:** Understands this of Christ's coming in the flesh: "There were none that would receive, nor even come to him, but hid their faces from him." The "drying up of the sea" refers to the Red Sea crossing; Christ's rebuking of the sea (Mt 8:26) shows the same divine power. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Why, when I came and announced deliverance from Babylon, was there no response?… Is it that my power was doubted?… What I have once done I can do again. If I delivered from Egypt, I can redeem from Babylon." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Spurgeon:** Christ came when "there practically seemed to be none left on the earth who were good for anything," and even though He "came in love and tenderness, there were none to answer to Him." (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons47/sermons47.xxxi.html)
- **Ellicott:** The "coming" of Jehovah must be taken in all its width — in deliverance from Babylon, in promise of greater blessings, and "in the fullest sense, in and through His Servant." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)
- **Guzik:** Guzik notes two possible interpretations: (a) "Where is the man who will stand up for Israel? Who will contend their case before God?" or (b) "Here the Lord compares Himself to a man… who is treated shamefully by his own wife and children. When he came home, there was no one to welcome him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)

---

### v. 3 — "I clothe the heavens in black and make sackcloth their covering."

**Traditional reading:** God asserts His power over the cosmos — He can darken the heavens as a sign of judgment or mourning. Some connect this to the darkness at Christ's crucifixion.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "God means to assert his power of leaving all nature in absolute darkness, if he so choose — a power necessarily belonging to him who said, 'Let there be light; and there was light.'" The Egyptian plague of darkness is not adequate to the language here. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Spurgeon:** Relates this directly to the crucifixion: "The last miracle recorded here… was performed by our Lord even when he was in his death agony. We read that, at high noon, the sun was veiled, and there was darkness over all the land for three black hours. Wonder of wonders, he who hung bleeding there had wrought that mighty marvel!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/) (quoted by Guzik)
- **Guzik:** "Heaven is in mourning, because of the sin and unbelief of God's people." Quotes Redpath: "Sin in the lives of God's people clothes heaven with blackness and sackcloth." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)
- **Gill:** Notes the possible reference to the three days' darkness in Egypt (Ex 10:12), but also connects it to the darkness at Christ's crucifixion (Mt 27:45) and to the fall of the pagan empire signified by the sun becoming black as sackcloth (Rev 6:12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)

---

### v. 4 — "The Lord GOD has given Me the tongue of discipleship, to sustain the weary with a word…"

**Traditional reading:** The Servant (Messiah) speaks. The Father has given Him a trained, disciple's tongue to speak timely words of comfort to the weary. Morning by morning the Father awakens Him to listen as a true disciple. This is the third Servant Song.

- **Gill:** "The words are to be understood of Christ… being anointed by the Spirit of the Lord God… he was abundantly qualified for the discharge of his prophetic office." The "word in season" is the Gospel: "which proclaims pardon, preaches peace… and invites weary ones to him for rest." The "morning by morning" awakening "seems to denote both the earliness in which Christ entered on his prophetic office, and his attentiveness in hearkening to all that was said in the eternal council and covenant by his divine Father." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "The Lord God hath given me the tongue of the learned; literally, the tongue of disciples; i.e. a trained tongue, a well-taught tongue. Christ 'did nothing of himself; as the Father had taught him,' so he spoke (John 8:28)." God held "immediate and constant communication with the 'Servant' — not enlightening him occasionally… but continually whispering in his ear." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "The daily teaching of the morning communion with God is contrasted by implication with the dreams and night visions of a less perfect inspiration. An illustration, perhaps a conscious fulfilment, may be found in Mark 1:35; Luke 4:42." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)
- **Guzik:** "The Messiah could speak with the tongue of the learned because in daily time with God He learned to hear as the learned." This verse describes the Messiah's "daily, wonderful, deep fellowship with God the Father." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)

---

### v. 5 — "The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious…"

**Traditional reading:** The "opening" of the ear is understood through the lens of the bondslave ceremony of Exodus 21:5-6, where a servant who loved his master had his ear pierced (opened) with an awl against the doorpost as a sign of lifelong, voluntary service. The Servant was not rebellious but perfectly obedient.

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Some understand this of the boring of the ear for perpetual service (Psalm 40:6; Exodus 21:6)." Contrasts the true Servant with Israel: "They did not hear; their ear was not opened; they were treacherous and rebellious from the womb" (Isa 48:8). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Gill:** "The allusion seems to be to the servant that had his ears bored, being willing to serve his master for ever, Exodus 21:5… It is expressive of his voluntary obedience, as Mediator, to his divine Father." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Guzik:** "This speaks of the total submission of the Messiah to the Lord GOD… This was a commitment not motivated by debt or obligation, only love for the master." Psalm 40:6 ("my ears You have opened") speaks of the same ceremony. Jesus was "a perfect bond-slave to the Father (Philippians 2:7)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)
- **Ellicott:** The Servant "accepts willingly" the suffering announced to Him in His morning communings with God, "because it is his Father's will." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)

---

### v. 6 — "I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard…"

**Traditional reading:** This is a precise prophetic description of the sufferings of Jesus Christ — scourging, beard-plucking, and spitting — all accepted voluntarily. Though the Gospels do not explicitly mention beard-plucking, the prophecy fills in that detail.

- **Spurgeon:** Devoted an entire sermon ("The Shame and Spitting") to this verse. "Of whom speaketh the prophet this?… We have before us the language of prophecy, but it is as accurate as though it had been written at the moment of the event." He highlights Christ's voluntary passivity: "I gave My back" — "He did not struggle; He did not seek to escape." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/isaiah-50.html)
- **Gill:** References the scourging ordered by Pilate (Mt 27:26), the plucking of the beard (a "great indignity and affront"), and the spitting in His face (Mt 26:67). Notes that spitting in the face was considered an extreme insult in the ancient world. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Plucking off the hair was not unknown to the Jews as a punishment (see Nehemiah 13:25)." "Spitting in the East marked at once contempt and abhorrence. It is a practice which continues to the present day." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Guzik:** "This prophecy speaks in chilling detail of the sufferings of the Messiah… There is no specific mention in the gospels of those who plucked out the beard of Jesus as part of His pre-crucifixion suffering, but from this passage in Isaiah we know it happened." Quotes Spurgeon: "Many of us could give to Christ all our health and strength… but when it comes to a point of reputation we feel the pinch." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)
- **Ellicott:** Traces the suffering-Servant motif through Scripture: the writer of Psalm 22:7, the much-enduring Job (Job 30:10), Jeremiah (Jer 20:7) "were but foreshadowings of the sufferings that should fall on him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)

---

### v. 7 — "Because the Lord GOD helps Me, I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set My face like flint…"

**Traditional reading:** Despite the suffering, the Servant has absolute confidence in divine help. "Setting His face like flint" expresses resolute, determined courage — not passive resignation. This was fulfilled in Luke 9:51 when Jesus "steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem."

- **Spurgeon:** Preached an entire sermon ("The Redeemer's Face Set Like a Flint") on this verse. Notes that Christ's resolve was tested "by offers from the world… by the persuasions of His friends… by the unworthiness of His clients… by the bitterness of the first few drops of suffering in Gethsemane… by the ease at which He could have backed out… by the taunts of those who mocked Him… by the full stress and agony of the cross." Yet it was sustained "by His divine schooling… by His conscious innocence… by His unshakable confidence in the help of God… by the joy that was set before Him." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-redeemers-face-set-like-a-flint)
- **Gill:** "Hardened against all opposition; resolute and undaunted; constant and unmoved by the words and blows of men; not to be browbeaten, or put out of countenance." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Servant's face is made "hard, impassive, expressionless, and at the same time determined, fixed not to give way (comp. Ezekiel 3:8, 9)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Guzik:** "There are two kinds of courage – the courage of the moment, which requires no previous thought, and a 'planned' courage, which sees the difficulty ahead and steadfastly marches towards it. Jesus had this kind of courage." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)
- **Ellicott:** "That one stay [the Lord God's help] gives to the suffering Servant an indomitable strength." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)

---

### v. 8 — "The One who vindicates Me is near. Who will dare to contend with Me? …"

**Traditional reading:** The Servant challenges all accusers, knowing God is His justifier. This anticipates Romans 8:33-34: "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies."

- **Pulpit Commentary:** "God, who knows his innocence, is near at hand, and will shortly 'make his righteousness clear as the noonday.' This was done when God raised up from the dead 'the Holy One and the Just' (Acts 3:14)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Gill:** "His Father was 'near' him in his whole state of humiliation… and 'justified' him from all the calumnies of his enemies… which is evident by his resurrection from the dead, by his ascension to heaven, and session at the right hand of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Spurgeon:** "Christ is innocent and, therefore, He defies all His accusers. Christ has suffered the penalty of the sin which He bore on our behalf, but He has so completely put it away that, notwithstanding our guilt, He defies all our accusers." (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons47/sermons47.xxxi.html)
- **Guzik:** "This is the Messiah's way of anticipating the truth of Romans 8:31: If God is for us, who can be against us?… the reason why Romans 8:31 applies to us is that it first applies to Jesus, and we are in Christ." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)

---

### v. 9 — "Surely the Lord GOD helps Me. Who is there to condemn Me? See, they will all wear out like a garment…"

**Traditional reading:** A restatement of confidence: God is the helper; no one can condemn the Servant. His enemies will decay like moth-eaten clothing.

- **Gill:** "Behold, the Lord God will help me — This is repeated from v. 7 to show the certainty of it, the strength of his faith in it, and to discourage his enemies." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "God will help the innocent, whom he has acquitted, and will destroy the accuser by a secret but most sure destruction. The moth shall eat them up (comp. Psalm 39:11, and Isaiah 51:8)." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "'They all shall wax old as a garment' — An echo of Job 13:28; Psalm 102:26; reproduced in Isaiah 51:6." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)

---

### v. 10 — "Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of His Servant? … Let him trust in the name of the LORD…"

**Traditional reading:** The Servant (or the LORD) now addresses the faithful remnant. Even the one who fears God and obeys the Servant's voice may walk in darkness — seasons of spiritual desolation and affliction. The counsel is simple: trust in the LORD and lean on God, even when no light is visible.

- **Gill:** "That walketh in darkness… not only in affliction and misery… but in desertion, under the hidings of God's face… 'Let him trust in the name of the Lord' — and to trust in him, when in the dark, is a glorious act of faith; this is believing in hope against hope." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Every such person is bidden to put aside his doubts, and trust wholly in the Name of the Lord, and stay upon his God. Hence light will shine in upon him." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Ellicott:** "All true servants know what it is to feel as if the light for which they looked had for a time failed them… The Servant felt it when he uttered the cry, 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)
- **Spurgeon:** "Let not the darkness keep you back any more than it did your Master — still go on, and rely upon your God." (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons47/sermons47.xxxi.html)
- **Guzik:** "The Messiah guides His people into the path of light. Simply, trust in the name of the LORD and rely upon your God. It isn't necessarily easy, but it certainly is simple." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)
- **Gill** notes that "His Servant" in this verse is the Messiah: some Jewish writers identify this servant as "Metatron" — "a name of the Messiah with them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)

---

### v. 11 — "Behold, all you who kindle a fire … walk in the light of your fire … You will lie down in a place of torment."

**Traditional reading:** A stark warning to those who refuse God's light and instead kindle their own "fire" — their own schemes, self-righteousness, man-made religion, or worldly comforts. The end of such self-reliance is torment.

- **Gill:** "Who, rejecting Christ the Light of the world, and despising the glorious light of his Gospel… set up the light of nature and reason as the rule of faith and practice; or the traditions and doctrines of men… or their own righteousness for their justification before God." The verse is "an ironical expression, bidding them take all the comfort and satisfaction they could" from their own works; but the outcome is to "lie down in sorrow." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The persons intended are "those whose tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity" (James 3:6), who cause strife. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/50.htm)
- **Ellicott:** Two meanings are suggested: (1) man's fiery wrath that works not the righteousness of God; (2) man's attempt to rest in earthly comforts or enjoyments instead of in God's light. The "sparks" may also be rendered "firebrands" — calumnies and execrations as weapons of warfare (cf. Eph 6:16). "Ye shall lie down in sorrow — the words point to a death of anguish, perhaps to the torment that follows death (comp. Luke 16:24)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/isaiah-50.html)
- **Guzik:** Connects the "fire" to "the profane fire of Nadab and Abihu described in Leviticus 10:1" — self-started worship not commanded by God. "This follows along the line of the Messiah's exhortation to trust in the name of the LORD, and not in our own efforts before God, which are like a profane fire." Quotes Motyer: "Torment… is only found here but its verb guarantees its meaning of grief, pain and displeasure – even the 'place of pain' – specifically the pains of sin under the curse of God." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-50/)
- **Spurgeon:** "Listen to this, you who live without God, yet think yourselves happy! You who have no hope of the great hereafter, yet are content with the present!… 'Walk in the light of your fire and in the sparks that you have kindled.' Be happy while you may!… This shall you have of My hand — you shall lie down in sorrow." (https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons47/sermons47.xxxi.html)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

From the sources I was able to access, there was broad agreement among the traditional Protestant commentators on the meaning of this chapter — all read it Christologically (the Servant = Jesus). I did not find substantial denominational disputes on this chapter. However, some nuances emerged:

- **Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill):** Strong emphasis on the particularity of Christ's substitutionary suffering and the doctrine of election. Gill reads v. 10's "who fears the LORD" as evidence that "there are none that naturally fear the Lord, only such who have the grace bestowed on them; their number is but small." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-50.html)
- **Anglican (Ellicott):** A more restrained, philologically precise approach, noting the Hebrew text carefully. Focus on the Servant as both ideal Israel and messianic figure, with an eye to literary echoes throughout Scripture.
- **Reformed / Evangelical (Precept Austin, Guzik):** Strong emphasis on covenant theology — God cannot ultimately divorce His covenant people. Guzik draws application for the believer's daily devotional life from v. 4 (morning-by-morning awakening).
- **Charismatic (Guzik / Enduring Word):** While Guzik is broadly evangelical, his emphasis on the Holy Spirit's application and the believer's call to courage and boldness reflects charismatic sensibilities without being distinctive on doctrinal points in this chapter.
